Here is a focused 3-week peaking block designed to taper volume, maintain/intensify intensity, and leave the lifter fresh for meet day. This plan assumes the client has a solid training base, is comfortable with the competition lifts (squat, bench, deadlift), and can handle a typical powerlifting-style program in a full gym. If needed, I’ve labeled substitutions and tweaks for equipment or minor preferences.

Assumptions
- Meet in 21 days from start of block (week 1 = day 1 of taper).
- Last 12 weeks were accumulation; this block is purely peaking with very limited volume.
- Primary lifts: squat (low-bar or high-bar as per preference), bench press, deadlift (conventional or sumo).
- Access to full gym means you can perform all main, back-off, and accessories safely.
- Nutritional plan: high-tensity days fueled, simple carb timing around lifts; hydration optimized; sleep target 7–9 hours.

Program structure (3 weeks)
- Week 1 (Deload/Volume Reduction + Intensification Tuning): Reduce volume by 40–50% from typical heavy week; maintain intensity near 90–95% 1RM for main lifts with 2–4 sets per lift; introduce slight technique emphasis and stimulus without fatiguing CNS.
- Week 2 (Peak Conditioning): Two lighter sessions with higher intensity, positive volume management, fewer sets; include practice attempts at or near planned opener/max effort ranges; prioritize technique under fatigue control.
- Week 3 (Meet Week / Taper): Final taper; singles or doubles at openers or predicted attempts, minimal volume, full recovery, last heavy peak before meet, priority on sleep, nutrition, and mental readiness. Day-before or day-of adjustments as needed.

Note on attempts: For meet day, plan a conservative opener attempt for each lift, plus a plan B if performance improves or worsens. Provide ranges but finalize with the athlete on the day of the meet.

Week-by-week plan (3 weeks)

Week 1 — Deload with Intensification Tuning (reduce volume, keep stimulus)
Goals: refresh CNS, maintain bar speed, reinforce technique, maintain RPE around 7–8 for main lifts.

Daily structure: 4 training days (3 main lifts per session + accessories). Alternate emphasis to ensure recovery.

Day 1 — Squat emphasis
- Warm-up: 10–12 minutes general + mobility for hips ankles
- Back Squat: 3 sets x 3 reps @ 88–92% 1RM (RPE 8–8.5); focus on bar path and depth
- Pause Squat (or tempo variation) optional: 2 sets x 2 reps @ 70–75% 1RM for technique and stiffness, 3-second pause at bottom (if you choose pause)
- Front Squat or Goblet squat alternative: 2 sets x 5 reps @ 60–65% 1RM (to maintain squat pattern)
- Accessory (choose 2–3):
  - Romanian Deadlift: 3 x 6 @ moderate weight
  - Leg Press or Belt Squat: 3 x 8–10
  - Core: 3 x 12 anti-rotation or planks
- Mobility/Primer: 5–8 minutes

Day 2 — Bench emphasis
- Warm-up: Band work, dumbbell presses, shoulder mobility
- Bench Press: 3 sets x 3 reps @ 88–92% 1RM
- Paused Bench (optional): 2 sets x 2 reps @ 75–80% 1RM, 2-second pause
- Floor Press or Close-Grip Bench: 2 x 4 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Accessory:
  - Overhead Press (or DB OTA): 3 x 6
  - Triceps work: pushdowns or dips 3 x 8–12
  - Lats/Chest accessory: 2–3 sets
- Mobility/Shoulder prehab: 5–8 minutes

Day 3 — Deadlift emphasis
- Warm-up: hip encouraging movements
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 3 reps @ 88–92% 1RM
- Deficit Deadlift or Block Pull variation (optional): 2 sets x 2 reps @ 70–75% 1RM
- Glute/Hamstring focus: 3 x 6–8
- Core: 3 x 12
- Back accessory: 2–3 sets of rows (DB or cable)

Day 4 — Full Body/Accessories
- Light technique day with not much loading
- Squat or bench technique work at 60–70% 1RM: 3 x 3
- DB Incline or Chest Fly: 3 x 8–12
- Rows: 3 x 8
- Grip/Forearms: 2–3 sets
- Mobility and recovery.

Notes Week 1:
- Keep total volume 40–50% lower than last heavy week.
- Focus on speed with loads near 90% 1RM; avoid grind.
- Sleep, nutrition, and hydration optimized; sparing use of caffeine, if any, before training; avoid heavy cardio.

Week 2 — Peak Conditioning (increase intensity, lower volume)
Goals: raise intensity to near-open or opener planning; maintain technique; progress toward 1–2 planned attempts.

Day 1 — Squat focus
- Warm-up: dynamic mobility
- Squat: 3 sets x 2 reps @ 90–93% 1RM
- Back-off sets: 2 x 2 @ 85–88% 1RM (optional if fatigue allows)
- Tempo/Paused work: 1 x 2 @ 70% 1RM (2-second pause)
- Accessory: 2–3 moves
  - Leg extension: 3 x 8–10
  - Abs: 3 x 12

Day 2 — Bench focus
- Warm-up: shoulder activation
- Bench: 3 sets x 2 reps @ 90–93% 1RM
- Paused Bench: 2 x 2 @ 80–85% 1RM
- Light close-grip or floor press: 2 x 3 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Accessory: 2–3 moves
  - DB incline: 3 x 8
  - Triceps extension: 3 x 10
  - Rows or rear delt work: 3 x 8–12

Day 3 — Deadlift focus
- Warm-up
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 2 reps @ 90–93% 1RM
- Speed pulls (optional): 2 x 1 @ 60–70% 1RM, focus on bar speed
- Glute/hamstring accessory: 3 x 6–8
- Core: 3 x 12

Day 4 — Technique + light volume
- Light technique day for all three lifts at 60–70% 1RM
- Mobility and recovery work
- Optional cardio or light conditioning 15–20 minutes at easy pace

Notes Week 2:
- Target 2-rep max range for main lifts; emphasize control and speed.
- Do not grind; avoid heavy RPE spikes.
- Start tapering accessory volume if needed to keep fresh.

Week 3 — Meet Week (full taper, singles/doubles near openers)
Goal: fresh, crisp technique, load management, mental readiness, ensure body is recovered. Very low fatigue.

Day 1 — Light technical practice
- Squat: 2 sets x 2 reps @ 70–75% 1RM
- Bench: 2 sets x 2 reps @ 70–75% 1RM
- Deadlift: 2 sets x 2 reps @ 70–75% 1RM
- Very light accessory work: 1–2 sets per movement, 6–8 reps
- Mobility and recovery work

Day 2 — Opener practice
- Squat: 1 set x 2 reps @ 85–90% 1RM, then 1 single at 95% 1RM if feeling good
- Bench: 1 set x 2 reps @ 85–90% 1RM, then 1 single at 95% 1RM if feeling good
- Deadlift: 1 set x 2 reps @ 85–90% 1RM, then 1 single at 95% 1RM if feeling good
- No back-off sets; emphasis on bar speed and technique
- Short mobility

Day 3 — Travel and meet prep
- Light movement, mobility work, mental rehearsal
- Nail sleep schedule; set up gear, check weigh-in readiness

Day 4 — Meet day (or cation)
- If meet day: perform planned opener attempts with 1–2 warm-up sets to get to first attempt
- Have clear plan:
  - Squat: Openers at 85–90% of best training, then a planned second at 95% if confidence
  - Bench: Openers at 85–90% of best training
  - Deadlift: Openers at 85–90% of best training
- If no meet, replicate meet day sequence with technique focus.

Nutrition and recovery components
- Daily protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg bodyweight to preserve lean mass during taper.
- Carbohydrate intake: moderate to high around training days to maintain performance; on lighter days, reduce slightly to align with energy needs.
- Hydration: aim for clear urine color; maintain electrolyte balance, especially around high-intensity days.
- Sleep: target 7–9 hours; create a consistent bedtime routine; consider a short nap if possible after intense sessions.
- Supplements (optional): caffeine timing around sessions (up to 200–400 mg), creatine 3–5 g daily (or 0.3 g/kg), beta-alanine if used in the past without GI issues; discuss with the athlete.
- Recovery: prioritize mobility work, mobility sessions, foam rolling, and light cardio (15–20 minutes) on lighter days to promote blood flow and recovery.
- Taper considerations: reduce volume significantly while maintaining intensity to preserve neural drive; avoid introducing new exercises.

Programming notes
- 1RM baselines: Use the lifter’s current best-lift 1RM to set percentages; if 1RM is unknown or likely to have improved recently in training, base off latest estimated max or last heavy attempt.
- Intensity bands: Keep main lifts around 88–93% for Week 1-2; Week 3 singles or doubles near 85–95% with explosive intent.
- Volume tuning: Week 1: -40 to -50% volume compared to heavy week; Week 2: -20 to -30% volume; Week 3: minimal, focusing on technique and nervous system freshness.
- Technique: Prioritize perfect form; if any pain or technique breakdown arises, reduce weight and address form.

Optional substitutions
- If gym lacks incline bench, replace with machine incline or DB incline press with same rep scheme.
- If deadlift variation is not available, perform hip hinge movements ( Romanian Deadlift or Kettlebell Swings) to maintain posterior chain stiffness.
- If you cannot perform pause squats due to equipment, perform tempo squats or tempo bench to maintain control.

Safety tips
- Ensure warm-up is thorough; use mobility and activation before main lifts.
- Keep a scale for plan adjustments if you feel unusually fatigued; dial back if necessary.
- Have a spotter/coach on bench and squat to ensure safety during heavy attempts.

Final notes
- This 3-week block is designed to maximize freshness, maintain strength, and leverage high-intensity exposure to perform well on meet day. If you want, I can tailor the plan to the lifter’s exact 1RM numbers, preferred equipment (e.g., sumo vs conventional deadlift), and schedule (training days per week, travel, weigh-in times).

Great idea. Adding light, competition-day prep cardio can help with recovery, insulin sensitivity, and overall readiness without adding fatigue. I’ve integrated short, easy cardio blocks into the 3-week peaking plan, positioned to minimize CNS or muscular load while still providing benefits.

Key principles
- Keep intensity very low; keep effort < RPE 3–4.
- Use brief sessions on non-critical days or after lighter lifting blocks.
- Favor low impact, zone 1–2 work or very light tempo cardio.
- Total cardio time added should be about 20–30 minutes per week, spread across the block.

Updated Week-by-Week Plan with Competition-Day Prep Cardio

Week 1 — Deload with Intensification Tuning (reduced volume, maintain stimulus)
- Additions: 2 optional 10–12 minute light cardio bouts per week (non-lift days or after light lifting)
  - Modality: brisk walk on treadmill, easy cycle, or elliptical at a very comfortable pace.
  - Intent: promote blood flow, aid recovery, minimal fatigue.

Week 2 — Peak Conditioning (intensity near opener planning, lower volume)
- Additions: 2 short cardio sessions, 8–12 minutes each, on non-lift days or after lighter accessory work
  - Modality: same as Week 1; keep speed easy, keep conversation pace.
  - Optional: 5 minutes easy incline walk on general warm-up days for micro-circulation if you have a flexible schedule.
- If scheduling is tight, you can place a single 12-minute cardio bout after Day 4 (Technique + Light Volume) to promote recovery without taxing muscles.

Week 3 — Meet Week / Taper (full taper, singles/doubles near openers)
- Additions: 1–2 micro cardio sessions totaling 8–12 minutes across the week
  - Day-before meet: a 6–8 minute easy walk or cycle to promote circulation and relaxation, not to induce fatigue.
  - Optional post-lift recovery cardio: 4–6 minutes easy cycling or walking after very light lifting on Day 1 or Day 2 to aid recovery and reduce stiffness.
- Rationale: keep joints lubricated and blood flowing without elevating fatigue or interfering with sleep.

Examples of 1–2 weekly cardio templates (adjust to schedule)
- Template A (after training, light session):
  - 8–12 minutes total: 2 minutes easy warm-up pace + 6–8 minutes steady easy pace + 2 minutes easy cooldown.
  - Modality: treadmill walk at 3–4 mph with 0–1% incline, or cycling at a gentle cadence (60–70 RPM) with low resistance.
- Template B (alone day):
  - 10–12 minutes total: 5 minutes easy walk + 5–7 minutes easy cycle, restore with 2 minutes of gentle mobility.

Nutrition and recovery alignment with cardio
- Hydration: maintain fluids around cardio sessions; electrolytes if training days are hot or long.
- Nutrition around cardio: keep pre- and post-workout nutrition aligned with lifts; if cardio is on a non-lift day, it can be done in a fasted or fed state based on preference, but avoid triggering hunger that disrupts meal timing.
- Sleep: cardio sessions should not push late in the day if it disrupts sleep; aim to finish cardio at least 2–3 hours before bedtime on those days.

Safety considerations
- Avoid high-impact or high-speed cardio that might accumulate fatigue or risk joint irritation close to meet.
- If any joint pain or aberrant fatigue arises, scale back or skip cardio that week.
- Ensure cardio does not interfere with warm-ups for main lifts or reduce training quality.

If you’d like, I can tailor these cardio blocks to the client’s actual schedule (days per week, travel, weigh-in times) and preferred modalities (treadmill, bike, rower, or air bike) and specify exact durations aligned with their 1RM-based plan.

Short answer: keep the cue, but tune how you train it in a peaking block.

Rationale
- The cue to “pull shoulders together” (retract scapulae, depress/depressors, tight upper back) is a foundational technique for bench setup, stability, and bar path. In peaking, you want to preserve technique that supports efficiency and safety while minimizing fatigue or overthinking.
- In a taper, you should avoid introducing too many new cues or spending excessive time on technique work that disrupts neuromuscular readiness. If the cue is already helping her setup and bar control, it’s worth drilling in a focused, low-fatigue way.

How to integrate in a 3-week peaking block
- Week 1 (deload/intensification tuning): Keep the cue in the warm-up and setup routine. Do 1–2 quick, low-fatigue drills per bench session to reinforce scapular retraction without adding volume.
  - Example drill: light banded pull-aparts or YTWL scapular retractions for 2–3 sets of 8–12 reps during warm-up.
  - Bench setup routine: 1–2 cues max (e.g., “shoulders tight and packed,” “elbows tucked slightly”); ensure tempo remains smooth.
- Week 2 (peak conditioning): If the cue helps with arch, bar control, and speed, keep it but keep it ultra-tidy, not cognitive overload.
  - Use a simple pre-lift checklist: feet set, hips/shoulders synced, scapulae retracted, grip width confirmed, grip tightness.
  - Replace or pair with a brief scapular-prone activation 1–2 sets x 5 reps before heavier sets if needed, but avoid extra volume.
- Week 3 (meet week): limit cue work to micro-adjustments only if there’s noticeable inefficiency.
  - For example, before singles, do a 1-minute “reset drill” focusing on scapular position in the setup, then proceed with warm sets. No heavy cueing during top singles.

Practical options
- If the cue is already helping, keep a single, consistent cue: “pull shoulders together and back.” Use it as part of your warm-up and setup routine only.
- If the lifter reports it causes tension or overthinking, simplify to a single cue or breathe-and-retrieve moment: cue a tight upper back as part of the lift’s setup without overloading cognitive load.
- Consider video feedback for 15–20 seconds before a top warm-up set to confirm scapular position and tuck, rather than continuous instruction during work sets.

When to adjust
- If performance shows a drop in bar speed or increased elbow/shoulder discomfort in the final week, revisit scapular control with a very brief drill (2 sets of 4–6 reps) and then return to the lift.

Bottom line
- Yes, drill it if it’s helping stability and bar feel, but keep it simple and low-fatigue in a peaking block. Use minimal cues, short drills, and integrate into warm-ups rather than turning it into a full technique block during heavy work. If you want, I can tailor a micro-cue drill you can slot into Week 1–3 with exactly sets/reps and timing.

Here’s a concise, competition-day morning plan tailored for a powerlifting meet. It focuses on warmups, opener timing, and smooth transitions to each lift, with buffers for travel/ weigh-in if needed. Adapt to your athlete’s exact meet schedule (order of lifts, weigh-in times, and warm-up room layout).

Overall principles
- Start early enough to accommodate travel, weigh-in, warm-up, and any delays, but avoid overdoing the morning.
- Keep warm-ups light but specific to each lift; avoid fatiguing sets before opening attempts.
- Maintain a calm routine, with a clear sequence and time cues for each step.
- Hydration and nutrition are aligned with lifting window; small steady energy before opening is ideal.
- Have a backup plan for missed attempts or delays (opener substitutions, extra warm-up time).

Suggested morning timeline (assuming the athlete has weigh-in earlier in the day and the meet starts in the late morning/afternoon)
- 6–7 hours before the first lift (or ~2–3 hours before weigh-in, adjust to meet schedule)
  - Wake with a light alarm, hydrate (sips of water with electrolytes if available).
  - Light mobility and breath work (5–8 minutes): ankle/knee hip circles, thoracic openers, hip flexor latches.
  - Breakfast: easily digestible, familiar meal with some carbs and protein (e.g., oats with fruit and a small yogurt, or toast with peanut butter and banana). 300–500 kcal depending on appetite.
  - Caffeine: if used, a small dose (100–200 mg) with water, unless contraindicated.

- Weigh-in window (if earlier in the day)
  - If weigh-in is before warm-ups, have a light, quick carb source after weigh-in (e.g., juice, a piece of fruit, a small white bread snack) to begin fueling for lifts.
  - Hydration continue; consider electrolytes if long interval between weigh-in and lifting.

- 2–3 hours before first lift
  - First full warm-up per lift (squat, bench, or deadlift, depending on order). Do the exact order as meet format requires; typically, lifters follow their rotation plan.
  - General warm-up (5–7 minutes): light cardio (bike or brisk walk) if available, followed by dynamic mobility for hips, thoracic spine, shoulders.

- For each lift, plan a consistent warm-up ladder
  - Example bench warm-up ladder:
    - Barbell only (45 lbs/20 kg) x 15 reps
    - 95 lbs/45 kg x 8
    - 135 lbs/62 kg x 5
    - 155–165 lbs/70–75 kg x 3
    - 2–3 sets of 2 reps at around 80–90% of planned opener (as a confidence boost, not fatiguing)
  - For squat ladder:
    - Bar only x 10–12
    - 135–185 x 5
    - 225 x 3
    - 275 x 2
    - 1–2 singles at opener weight
  - For deadlift ladder:
    - Bar only x 8–10
    - 135–185 x 3
    - 225 x 2
    - 275 x 2
    - 1 single at opener weight
  - Time targets: each main lift warm-up should take roughly 6–12 minutes, with 1–2 minutes rest between attempts.

- Opener timing and openers
  - Aim to be in the warm-up room and prepared for opening attempts about 15–25 minutes before the scheduled opener.
  - Openers should be chosen well within the lifter’s trained range and not new or experimental on meet day.
  - After the opener, rest 3–5 minutes before attempt 2, then 3–5 minutes before the final attempt if applicable.

- If delays occur
  - Keep moving through the ladder with light, non-fatiguing reps to maintain warmth.
  - Use a short breathing reset and reset cues if anxious: 4 seconds inhale through the nose, 4 seconds exhale through the mouth.

- Between lifts
  - Nutrition: small snack (banana, crackers, a protein shake) every 60–90 minutes as needed; sip water consistently.
  - Mobility refresh: light shoulder blades/back activation, thoracic mobility to stay loose.
  - Mental cueing: 60–90 seconds of box breathing or a quick visualization for each lift.

- Final pre-try checks (about 10–15 minutes before each opener)
  - Suit/equipment check (wraps, belt, sleeves, lifter’s belt, knee sleeves): ensure all gear is legal and comfortable.
  - Brief warm-down: light breathing, 20–30 seconds of isometric holds (glute bridge, mid-back isometrics) to keep tension without fatigue.
  - Final cue: “tight, stable and ready” for the setup.

- On the platform
  - Use a consistent stance and grip as practiced.
  - Trust the openers; if any technique feels off, call a timeout if allowed to reset rather than forcing the attempt.

- Post-run/meet-day adjustments
  - If a lift goes significantly below opener, decide quickly whether to attempt a conservative second attempt or skip due to safety.
  - If a lift hits a good opening, follow the planned progression for second and third attempts.

Absolutely. Adding a deload between Week 1 and Week 2 of the 3-week peaking block can help address accumulated fatigue, reduce risk of technique breakdown, and preserve performance for the peak sessions. Here’s how to integrate a deload week and adjust the structure accordingly.

What changes
- Introduce a micro-deload between Week 1 (deload/intensification tuning) and Week 2 (peak conditioning).
- Keep main lifts and intent high, but reduce volume and slightly lower intensity to freshen the nervous system and joints without losing technique familiarity.
- Maintain competition-day prep cardio at a very light level, since it’s non-fatiguing.

Revised 3-week plan layout with a deload
- Week 1: Deload with Intensification Tuning (as previously outlined)
  - Volume reduced ~40–50% from a heavy week; intensity near 88–92% for main lifts; focus on speed and technique.
  - 4 training days; main lifts with 2–4 sets per lift.
  - 1–2 short scapular cue drills as needed; maintain the shoulder cue with minimal cognitive load.
  - Light competition-day prep cardio: 1–2 bouts of 8–12 minutes as described.
- Deload Week (Week 1.5): Short, very light recovery block
  - 3–4 training days, but with substantially reduced volume and lower intensity.
  - Main lifts: 2–3 sets of 2 reps at 70–75% 1RM, focusing on perfect technique and bar speed rather than heavy loading.
  - Fewer accessories: 1–2 movements per session, 2–3 sets of 6–8 reps, light loads.
  - No competition-day cardio beyond optional 5–8 minutes very light walking per session.
  - Mobility, tissue work, and brief scapular drills can be included, but keep them low-impact and short (5–8 minutes total per session).
- Week 2: Peak Conditioning
  - Rebuild intensity toward the upper end of 88–93% 1RM for main lifts with 3–4 sets of 2 reps.
  - Minimal back-off volume; focus on speed and technique with controlled rest.
  - 2–3 accessory moves to maintain technique without adding fatigue.
  - Competition-day prep cardio continues lightly (8–12 minutes per session, 1–2 sessions per week).
- Week 3: Meet Week / Taper
  - Maintain very light, crisp singles/doubles near opener weights.
  - Very low total volume; emphasis on freshness and sleep.
  - Final meet-day prep cardio kept minimal; avoid any fatigue risk.

Sample week-by-week with deload insertion

Week 1 — Deload with Intensification Tuning
- 4 days
  - Squat: 3 x 3 @ 88–92% 1RM
  - Bench: 3 x 3 @ 88–92% 1RM
  - Deadlift: 3 x 3 @ 88–92% 1RM
  - Accessories: 2–3 moves, 3 x 6–8
  - Light scapular drills: 2–3 sets of 8–12
  - Cardio: 2 x 8–12 minutes easy
- Focus: speed, technique, no grind.

Deload Week (Week 1.5)
- 3–4 days
  - Main lifts: 2–3 sets x 2 reps @ 70–75% 1RM
  - Accessory: 2 moves, 2–3 sets x 6–8
  - Minimal or no cardio
  - Cue maintenance for the bench cue as before, but keep it minimal
- Focus: recovery, technique consolidation, tissue work.

Here’s a practical, evidence-informed approach for the 48 hours before a powerlifting meet. It focuses on glycogen replenishment, hydration, sodium, and general GI comfort to support performance in the final push without causing GI distress or bloating.

Goals
- Maximize muscle glycogen stores (carbs) without creating GI upset.
- Maintain stable hydration and electrolyte balance.
- Keep sodium at a level that supports fluid retention and nerve/muscle function without causing bloating.
- Support sleep and recovery; avoid late heavy meals or anything new that could upset digestion.

Timeline and daily plan

48 hours before meet (start this plan as a general guideline the day before the meet’s weigh-in window if you’re closer to weigh-in, or the day before the meet if weigh-in is earlier)
- Carbohydrates: 5–7 g/kg bodyweight total for the day; distribute evenly across meals with a focus on complex carbs and some easily digestible carbs around workouts.
- Protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg total daily intake to support recovery and muscle protein synthesis.
- Fats: remaining calories after carbs and protein; keep fats moderate to support energy without delaying gastric emptying.
- Fluids: aim for 2.5–3.5 L/day (adjust for body size, climate, and sweat rate). Include a start-of-day water balance and steady intake throughout waking hours.
- Sodium: 3–5 g total sodium across the day is a practical target if you’re not markedly sensitive to salt. On heavy-sweat days or in hot environments, may go up to 6 g/day, but monitor for bloating.

Meal strategy
- Carbs: prioritize low-FODMAP, lower-fiber carbs in the 24 hours before the meet if GI sensitivity exists. Good options include:
  - Complex carbs: oats, rice, potatoes, pasta, quinoa, sourdough bread.
  - Simple carbs around workouts or if you train the same day: fruit (bananas, apples), fruit juice, sports drinks.
- Protein: distribute 4–6 meals with 25–40 g protein per meal, depending on total daily targets.
- Fat: keep moderate; avoid very large fatty meals right before bed if GI comfort is a concern.

Hydration and electrolytes
- Hydration plan:
  - Morning (before any training or weigh-in window): 500–750 ml water with a small pinch of salt or electrolyte tablet.
  - During the day: sip water consistently; aim to drink enough so urine is pale straw-colored.
  - If training or weigh-in is later in the day and you’ll be sweating, add an electrolyte drink (sodium-containing, 300–500 mg Na per serving) to replace losses.
- Sodium strategy:
  - Target roughly 3–5 g of sodium across the day as a baseline, adjusting up to 6 g if sweat rate is high (heavy garments, hot environment, or sweat testing indicates high loss).
  - Salt intake around meals can help with taste and fluid retention; pairing sodium with carbs can improve GI tolerance for some athletes.
- Potassium and other electrolytes:
  - Ensure potassium from foods (bananas, potatoes, leafy greens) daily, typically 2–3 g/day.
  - Magnesium and calcium as part of a balanced diet; avoid high-dose supplements right before bed if it disrupts sleep.

Meal timing ideas (example day)
- Breakfast: bowl of oats with a banana, honey, and a scoop of yogurt or milk; 25–40 g protein.
- Snack: fruit and a small yogurt or a plain bagel with peanut butter.
- Lunch: portion of lean protein (30–40 g), rice or potatoes, or pasta, with a moderate amount of vegetables.
- Pre-competition-light meal (if this occurs): easily digested carbs like white rice with chicken and a small serving of fruit; keep fat low to moderate.
- Dinner (evening): similar to lunch but slightly lighter if bed-time is near; ensure a final protein source to sustain overnight amino acids.

GI considerations and personal preferences
- If the athlete has a history of GI distress with high-carb meals, practice the same plan during training days (carb loading day-before meet) to identify tolerances.
- If you train the day prior to weigh-in or late in the day, you can adjust the timing to ensure you’re not overloading GI near bed-time.

Testing and adjustments
- If possible, trial this plan during a high-stress practice week or on a non-competition week to verify tolerance.
- Monitor:
  - Sleep quality: ensure not to overdo caffeine or heavy meals late.
  - GI: any bloating, gas, reflux; adjust carb timing or type if needed.
  - Hydration markers: urine color, thirst, and performance in any pre-meet warm-ups.

Pro tips
- Practice your “carb window” in training: have a predictable, tolerated carb source right after your main training session to normalize digestion and pacing.
- If weigh-in happens early in the day, raise carbs a bit more earlier to ensure glycogen is topped off by the time you lift.
- If weigh-in is late or you’re consuming a lot of fluid, consider pacing hydration to avoid a late bloating effect.

Here is a consolidated, 3-week meet-prep plan that incorporates all the adjustments discussed: deload between Week 1 and Week 2, a 95% single test mid-block (Week 2) for each lift, a light competition-day prep cardio plan, a bench cue handling approach during a peaking block, and the 48-hour nutrition/fluids plan framing (integrated but not duplicative). The plan is written week-by-week with day-level structure, including sets/reps, intent, and notes. You can drop in the athlete’s exact 1RM numbers and preferred lift variants (conventional vs sumo, high-bar vs low-bar) to customize percentages.

Assumptions for plan
- Meet is in 21 days from start of Week 1.
- Last 12 weeks were accumulation; Week 1 is a deload/intensification tuning, Week 1.5 is a deload micro-cycle, Week 2 is peak conditioning with a mid-block 95% single test, Week 3 is meet taper.
- Lifter: 28, female, intermediate recreational lifter; main lifts: Squat, Bench, Deadlift; options for stance/variation as per preference.
- 4 training days per week on Weeks 1–2; Week 3 tapers to 3–4 days depending on meet schedule.

Week 1 — Deload with Intensification Tuning
Goals
- Refresh CNS, maintain bar speed, reinforce technique, keep RPE around 7–8 on main lifts.
- Begin very light, controlled scapular cue reinforcement for bench if applicable.
- Introduce light, competition-day prep cardio.

Structure
- Frequency: 4 days (S, Bnch, Deadlift emphasis days, plus a light technique/accessory day)
- Main lifts intensity: 88–92% 1RM
- Volume: 3 sets x 3 reps for main lifts
- Accessory: 2–3 movements per session, 3 x 6–8
- Bench cueing: maintain “pull shoulders together/back” cue in warm-ups; minimal additional cueing during work sets

Week 1 - Sample Day Layout
Day 1 — Squat emphasis
- Warm-up: 10–12 minutes general + hip/ankle mobility
- Back Squat: 3 sets x 3 reps @ 88–92% 1RM
- Optional: Pause Squat (or tempo variation): 2 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM, 3-second bottom pause
- Front Squat or Goblet: 2 x 5 @ 60–65% 1RM
- Accessory (choose 2–3): Romanian Deadlift 3 x 6; Leg Press 3 x 8–10; Core 3 x 12
- Mobility/Primer: 5–8 minutes
- Cardio: optional 8–12 minutes easy (see cardio plan)

Day 2 — Bench emphasis
- Warm-up: Band work, shoulder activation
- Bench Press: 3 x 3 @ 88–92% 1RM
- Paused Bench (optional): 2 x 2 @ 75–80% 1RM
- Floor Press or Close-Grip: 2 x 4 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Accessory: Overhead Press 3 x 6; Triceps 3 x 10; Lats/Chest accessory 2–3 sets
- Bench cue integration as above
- Mobility: 5–8 minutes
- Cardio: optional 8–12 minutes

Day 3 — Deadlift emphasis
- Warm-up: hip-opening movements
- Deadlift: 3 x 3 @ 88–92% 1RM
- Deficit/Block Pull (optional): 2 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Glute/Hamstring focus: 3 x 6–8
- Core: 3 x 12
- Back accessories: 2–3 sets Rows
- Mobility: 5–8 minutes
- Cardio: optional 8–12 minutes

Day 4 — Light/Accessory + Technique
- Light technique work for all three lifts at 60–70% 1RM: 3 x 3
- Accessory: 2–3 moves (DB incline, rows, grip, core)
- Mobility/Recovery
- Optional light cardio 8–12 minutes

Notes
- Keep total weekly volume 40–50% below heavy-week benchmarks.
- Sleep, hydration, and nutrition optimized; limit new stimuli.

Week 1.5 — Deload Week (recovery micro-cycle)
Goals
- Recovery-focused; allow CNS/joints to refresh.
- Preserve technique familiarity; minimize fatigue.

Structure
- 3–4 training days; very light volume; 70–75% 1RM for 2 x 2 on main lifts
- Accessory: 2 movements, 2–3 sets x 6–8
- Cardio: minimal (optional 5–8 minutes very light walking per session)
- Bench scapular cue: reduce cognitive load; simple setup cues only if needed

Week 1.5 Sample Day Layout
Day A
- Squat: 2–3 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Optional: 2 x 2 @ 60–65% 1RM
- Accessory: 2 moves, 2–3 sets x 6–8
- Mobility and 5–8 minutes

Day B
- Bench: 2–3 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Optional: 1 x 2 @ 60–65% for speed
- Accessory: 2 moves, 2–3 sets x 6–8
- Debrief on cue usage if needed

Day C
- Deadlift: 2–3 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Optional: 1 x 2 @ 60–65%
- Accessory: 2 moves, 2–3 sets x 6–8

Day D
- Light technique day or cardio only
- Mobility and soft tissue work

Week 2 — Peak Conditioning with 95% Singles (mid-block test) plus 95% singles
Goals
- Test 95% singles for each lift to anchor openers and gauge true near-1RM capability.
- Two 90–93% doubles per lift; single 95% test; optional light back-off after the 95% singles
- Maintain technique and control; avoid grinding

Structure
- 4 training days with three lifts per day
- Main lifts: 3–4 x 2 @ 90–93% 1RM
- 95% singles: 1 x 1 @ 95% per lift (placed after a solid warm-up)
- Optional back-off: 2 x 2 @ 85–88% after the 95% singles if fresh
- Accessories: 2–3 moves, 6–8 reps
- Cardio: 8–12 minutes light, 1–2 sessions per week

Week 2 Sample Layout
Day A — Squat focus
- Warm-up: mobility, activation
- Squat: 3–4 x 2 @ 90–93%
- 95% single: 1 x 1 @ 95% (after 2–3 light sets; rest 3–5 minutes)
- Back-off: 2 x 2 @ 85–88% (optional)
- Accessory: 2–3 moves
- Cardio: 8–12 minutes light after or before as fits schedule

Day B — Bench focus
- Warm-up: shoulder activation
- Bench: 3–4 x 2 @ 90–93%
- 95% single: 1 x 1 @ 95%
- Optional back-off: 2 x 2 @ 85–88%
- Accessory: 2–3 moves
- Cardio: 8–12 minutes light

Day C — Deadlift focus
- Warm-up
- Deadlift: 3–4 x 2 @ 90–93%
- 95% single: 1 x 1 @ 95%
- Optional back-off: 2 x 2 @ 85–88%
- Accessory: 2–3 moves
- Cardio: 8–12 minutes light

Day D — Technique/Light + Recovery
- Light technique day for all lifts: 60–70% 1RM, 3 x 3
- Mobility and breathing

Notes on Week 2
- Place 95% singles after the main sets but before back-off or volume drops.
- Rest 3–5 minutes between 95% single and any subsequent set for the same lift.
- If 95% singles feel off, revert to the planned 90–93% doubles and treat the 95% as a diagnostic only.

Week 3 — Meet Week / Taper
Goals
- Very light singles/doubles near planned openers.
- Minimal volume; maximize recovery, sleep, and readiness.
- Maintain a crisp, fast setup and confidence in opening attempts.

Week 3 Sample Layout
Day A — Light technical practice
- Squat: 2 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Bench: 2 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Deadlift: 2 x 2 @ 70–75% 1RM
- Very light accessories
- Mobility

Day B — Opener practice
- Each lift: 1 x 2 @ 85–90% 1RM, then 1 x 1 @ 95% if feeling good
- No back-off sets; emphasize bar speed and clean setup
- Short mobility

Day C — Travel/Meet prep
- Light movement, mobility, mental rehearsal
- Sleep/Wake schedule optimization, weigh-in prep

Day D — Meet day
- Opener attempts as planned with 1–2 warm-up sets to hit first attempts
- Prepare for second/third attempts per meet plan
- Have contingency for delays; maintain calm routines and breathing

Nutrition and hydration integration (within Week 3)
- 48 hours pre-meet: follow the 48-hour plan
  - Carbs 5–7 g/kg/day, distributed; protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day
  - Fluids 2.5–3.5 L/day or tuned to personal sweat rate
  - Sodium: 3–5 g/day baseline; up to 6 g if sweating heavily
- Carbohydrate timing: favor complex carbs with some easily digestible carbs around workouts
- GI comfort: choose low-FODMAP options when necessary; test tolerance in Week 2 if possible
- Hydration: maintain pale urine; start the day with hydration, dose electrolytes around workouts if sweating

Bench cueing and technique notes (concise integration)
- If the “pull shoulders together/back” cue is useful and not fatiguing, keep it through Week 1; reduce cognitive load in Week 1.5 and Week 2; micro-adjust only in Week 3 if necessary.
- Use a brief, simple pre-lift checklist for bench: feet set, hips/shoulders aligned, scapular retraction, grip width determined, bar path clean, elbows tucked.
- No heavy cueing during top attempts; preserve rhythm and speed.

60-second contingency and safety
- If fatigue or technique deteriorates: scale back volume, maintain conditioning while preserving CNS; avoid grinding in Week 2.
- If any pain arises: drop the set, switch to lighter technique work, or substitute with safer variations.

Final note and customization options
- If you want me to tailor exact weekly loads to the athlete’s current 1RM and lift preferences (conventional vs sumo, high-bar vs low-bar), share:
  - Current bests for squat, bench, deadlift (and how they have progressed in the last 4–8 weeks)
  - Lift variant choices and any equipment substitutions
  - Weigh-in timing and travel constraints
  - Any known GI sensitivities or training-day constraints
I can output a fully formatted, minute-by-minute or hour-by-hour plan for Week 1 through Week 3 (with exact sets/reps, percentages, rest intervals) ready to hand to the lifter or to plug into your training calendar.
